Use it to find the stable core of a network across snapshots, replicates or conditions. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [graphs]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A non-empty list of graphs with the same directedness. None is modified. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph (a copy, if only one graph is given). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the list is empty or the graphs differ in directedness. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Equivalent to chaining `intersection()`. NetworkX's `intersection_all` keeps every node present in all graphs, even without surviving edges; EdgeCase follows `intersection()`, which keeps only endpoints of shared edges. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~intersection`) : Keep the edges common to two graphs. [](`~union_all`) : Combine any number of graphs. ## Examples {.doc-examples} `ec.friends()` is a network of friendships among the same 24 people in 2024, and `snapshot=2` gives the network a year later. In 2026 three of the 2025 friendships ended. The snapshots share their node IDs, so their intersection holds the friendships of all three years: ::: {#aafadfa4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec years = [ ec.friends(), ec.friends(snapshot=2), ec.friends(snapshot=2) .delete_edge("Dev", "Femi") .delete_edge("Gwen", "Lou") .delete_edge("Rosa", "Sven"), ] [year.count_edges() for year in years] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [43, 51, 48] ``` ::: ::: All 43 friendships of 2024 were still there in 2025, but three of them ended in 2026, so 40 are in all three years: ::: {#acd6ddcc .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph.intersection_all(years).count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 40 ``` ::: ::: [Transforming graphs](../user-guide/transforming.qmd#set-operations) compares the set operations, and explains why the graphs must number their nodes alike.
